# Work delegate

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
The only skill that makes the agent-led delivery offer and records the answer; after a yes it runs the team through the skill that owns each stage. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Look for a delivery choice that covers this goal: the item's `delivery` value, its Notes > Decisions and context, and its parent's choice. A sub-item makes no offer. A quick question, a small edit, or a small item (one or two tasks, no sub-items) gets no offer: record owner-led with the reason and go on (`references/agent-led-delivery.md`, section 1).
   `toolkit work show <id> --section 'Decisions and context'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led --note 'Small item: one or two tasks, so no delivery offer.'`
2. No choice recorded: add the offer as an Open Questions row, set the item waiting on the owner, and ask exactly this as the last line of the reply: "Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner?" "You drive" in his own words is already the answer.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| <next Q-id> | Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner? | delivery | Open | owner |'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
3. Yes: ask the team question. Where the host lets this chat list, read, and message other chats and offer new chats to the owner: "Do you want one team inside this chat, or do you want me to rename this chat to Main Orchestrator and coordinate other chats that each have their own team?" On any other host, say the multi-chat arrangement is not available here and ask: "Shall I run one team of helpers inside this chat?"
4. Main Orchestrator chosen: also ask "Do you want me to archive sessions after their task is fully complete, everything is merged and shipped, and you approved?"
5. Record the choice, the goal it covers, who said it, the date, the team arrangement, the archive answer, and the limits in Notes > Decisions and context; set the delivery value; hand the item back to the agent unless another of his questions is open; add one history note; read it back (`references/agent-led-delivery.md`, section 3).
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Decisions and context' --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Agent-led delivery accepted by <owner>: <his words>'`
6. No, or a later revoke: record it the same way, and set `waiting_on` to `agent` when the agent still works on the item. Do not offer again for this goal unless it grows a lot or the owner asks.
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
7. Run the team through the skill that owns each stage (`references/agent-led-delivery.md`, section 4; `references/team-arrangements.md`). The main agent plans, briefs the helpers, gives one writer per path, and is the only writer of the work item.
   `toolkit work list --tree`
8. Stop at every owner gate: set the item waiting on him and ask through the skill that owns the gate. Keep working on what the answer does not block.
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
9. Archive a chat only when its task is complete, merged and shipped, its report is saved, the owner approved it, and he said yes to archiving. Never delete a chat.
10. End every reply with the one question (the offer, the team question, or the next gate) or the exact words that continue ("Say 'go' and the team starts on P1.").

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- The offer and the team questions are asked word for word, in the reply text, never through a question tool.
- The `--delivery` command marks the offer's Open Questions row Answered and prints "Marked Q-xx Answered". Never edit that row by hand. When no other question for him is open, it also sets `waiting_on` to `none` ("It is no longer waiting on the owner"). Set `agent` right after it when the agent continues (steps 5 and 6); keep `owner` while another of his questions on the item is open.
- A sub-item is part of its parent's goal: creating it under the parent copies the parent's delivery value. Set it only when it is missing or differs, with a note naming the parent.
- The choice belongs to the named goal only. It does not carry over to another goal, a new item, or an unrelated sub-item.
- Acceptance alone starts no helpers; the team arrangement answer does. A no to the team question means no helpers.
- Delegation never widens merge, deployment, spending, or publishing. Every approval gate still applies, and approvals already given still count.
- Missing tracker access is not a missing decision. Keep an unsaved choice in the handoff and save it when access returns.
- A recorded lead or chat id is coordination information, not proof that an agent is still running.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Record the choice in the issue's Notes and a delivery label (`references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`).

## Agents

- `builder` (`references/agent-builder.md`), `researcher` (`references/agent-researcher.md`), and `acceptance-checker` (`references/agent-acceptance-checker.md`), briefed by the stage skill that uses them. # Agent-led delivery

The rules for the delivery offer: when to make it, the exact questions, how
to record the owner's answers, and what an acceptance allows. The four
questions keep their exact wording. The choice is recorded in the work item's
Notes > Decisions and context and in its `delivery` value, in every tracker.

## Contents

1. Offer once for the goal
2. Ask how the team is arranged
3. Record the choice
4. Divide responsibility

## 1. Offer once for the goal

First read the item's `delivery` value and its Notes > Decisions and context
to see whether the owner already accepted, declined, or revoked agent-led
delivery for this goal. `not-offered` means no answer is recorded yet. Do not
treat missing access as an undecided choice. When the records show no choice,
ask exactly:

> Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner?

`work-delegate` is the only skill that makes this offer or records its
answer. `work-on`, `work-decide`, and the session briefing only point at it,
so the owner is asked once, in one place.

Do not make this offer for a simple question or quick edit, or for a small
item (one or two tasks, no sub-items): record owner-led at once, with the
reason, so the briefing stops listing the offer as an agent to-do.

```text
toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led --note 'Small item: one or two tasks, so no delivery offer.'
```

The offer is made once, at the top item of the goal; a sub-item is part of
its parent's goal. `toolkit work new --parent` copies the parent's delivery
value to a new sub-item and says so ("Delivery: agent-led, as recorded for
WI-012."). Check it, and make no offer for it. Only when the value is missing
or differs from the parent's, set it with a note naming the parent:

```text
toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led --note 'Part of WI-012, whose goal is agent-led.'
```

When you ask, first add the question as an Open Questions row (owner decides,
Affects `delivery`) and set the item waiting on the owner, so a later session
sees the offer is open if the answer does not come in this one:

```text
toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| <next Q-id> | Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner? | delivery | Open | owner |'
toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner
```

Ask it in the reply text, as its last line, never through a question tool.
Wait for the answer before taking responsibility for organizing delivery,
while continuing any useful work that does not depend on the choice. The
`--delivery` command that records his answer marks that row Answered and
prints "Marked Q-xx Answered"; do not edit the row by hand.

A clear acceptance authorizes agent-led delivery for this goal across
sessions. A later explicit request for agents to manage or deliver the goal
also counts ("you drive", "run with it", "take it from here"); do not ask the
offer question again. A decline keeps normal help and the usual record upkeep,
and stops the offer for this goal, including in later sessions. Offer again
only if the work grows a lot or the owner asks about agent-led delivery. The
owner may revoke acceptance at any time. Record it as revoked: agent-led
responsibility ends, normal help and record upkeep continue, and the same
rules as a decline apply.

The choice belongs to the named goal. It does not carry over to an unrelated
goal, a new work item, or an unrelated sub-item. The end of a session does not
end it, and missing tracker access does not mean the owner is undecided.

## 2. Ask how the team is arranged

After a clear acceptance, read the goal record for a saved team arrangement.
When none is recorded, ask one more question:

> Do you want one team inside this chat, or do you want me to rename this chat to Main Orchestrator and coordinate other chats that each have their own team?

Offer the multi-chat choice only where the current host lets this chat list,
read, and message other chats and offer new chats to the owner as task
buttons. Check the tools this session has; do not assume. On any other host,
tell the owner the multi-chat arrangement is not available on this host and
ask one simple question instead:

> Shall I run one team of helpers inside this chat?

A yes is an arrangement choice: one team inside this chat. A no means the main
agent does the work itself. Record either answer with the goal.

Do not ask after a decline or a revocation, and do not ask again once the
owner's answer is recorded for the goal. The owner may change the arrangement
at any time; record the new answer.

When the owner chooses the Main Orchestrator arrangement, ask one more
question:

> Do you want me to archive sessions after their task is fully complete, everything is merged and shipped, and you approved?

Record the answer with the goal like the arrangement answer, and do not ask it
again.

`team-arrangements.md` explains what each answer means, including when a
chat may be archived. Read it before organizing the team, and when resuming a
goal that has a recorded arrangement.

## 3. Record the choice

Save accepted, declined, or revoked, and the team arrangement answer once
given, in the item:

- `toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led` for accepted;
  `toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led` for declined or revoked.
- When the offer's row was his last open question, the delivery command
  also sets `waiting_on` to `none` and prints "It is no longer waiting on the
  owner". When the agent continues the item (an acceptance, or a decline
  with work still to do), set it to `agent`:
  `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`. Keep `owner` while another of
  his questions on the item is open.
- A block in Notes > Decisions and context, written with
  `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Decisions and context' --set-file <file>`:

  ```markdown
  - **Agent-led delivery (WI-012 goal: CSV export):** accepted by Mike on
    2026-09-26 ("you drive, I'll approve things"). Team: one team inside this
    chat. Archive answer: not asked. Limits: no merge, deployment, spending, or
    publishing beyond what was given. Lead: this chat.
  ```

- One history note with the owner's words.

Record the goal scope, the state (accepted, declined, or revoked), the team
arrangement answer when one was given, the archive answer when it was asked,
who said it and the date, the limits, and which chat or agent leads delivery.
A lead reference coordinates ownership; it is not a lock and not proof that an
agent is still running. Read the saved section back and check the meaning
landed.

Keep the Overview Next action consistent with the choice. For example,
replace a pending "ask whether agents lead" next action once the owner
answers. Check the choice and the next action together; if only one save
worked, report the partial save and keep the exact fix as pending.

No item exists yet: create one through `work-on` when the goal warrants a
record. Never create an item only to record a refusal. With no place to save
it, say so and carry the choice in the handoff until it can be saved.

The main agent owns every change to the item. Helpers return findings and
proposed changes to it. Respect another main session's ownership, read shared
records again before editing, and settle conflicting ownership before
overwriting anything.

If the write fails, lead with "Not saved", name the destination and the
failed step, and keep the choice as a pending update. If the write worked but
the read-back failed, say "Saved but not verified". Continue independent work.
Put the pending save in the handoff and retry when access returns.

## 4. Divide responsibility

With acceptance, agents take responsibility for moving the agreed goal
through discovery, the owner interview, requirements, open questions, records,
focused research, design challenge, the authorized build, testing, and
delivery. They keep the plan and the Resume here note current and bring the
owner the decisions and results that need him.

The owner stays product owner: he makes product and scope decisions, gives
the required approvals, and approves the result. Acceptance does not widen
tool, security, spending, publishing, deployment, build, or any other existing
authority. Every project gate still applies, and approvals already given still
count.

Acceptance alone does not authorize starting helpers. The owner's choice of a
team arrangement does: it authorizes focused, bounded helper agents for that
goal only. It does not carry over to another goal, and every other limit on
tools, spending, publishing, deployment, and approvals still applies. A no to
the one-team question is not an arrangement and authorizes no helpers. Use
helpers only when that choice or other recorded authority allows them and
research, specialist knowledge, an independent check, or parallel work helps.
Every agent runs on Opus. Do not set up a fixed council, repeat reviews
without a new reason, or let helper rounds replace a decision.

Run each stage through the skill that owns it: `work-requirements`,
`solution-design`, `work-on`, `work-check`, `work-finish`. If a skill or an
agent is not available, the main agent does that part itself and records the
same decisions, evidence, and next action.

## Look before the first Git write

Other sessions may work in the same repository at the same time. Before the
first Git write in a session, run each of these on its own:

```text
git worktree list
git status
git remote
```

- `git remote` prints nothing: the project has no remote. Read "A project
  with no remote" below before any fetch, pull, push, or pull request.
- An unknown worktree, a branch that moved, or a change this session did not
  make means another session is working. Do not change it. Tell the owner.
- The shared primary checkout is the first entry `git worktree list` prints.
  In it, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never commit, push, rebase, or delete another session's branch, and never
  commit its uncommitted changes, even when they look finished.

Roadmap row. Each task field (`**Work:**`, `**Deliverable:**`,

```text
toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>
```

## 4. Status words and ticking a task

- Phase status: Not Started, In Progress, Done (Cancelled for a phase that
  was dropped). Use no other word, such as "Planned".
- Task status: Not Started, In Progress, Done, Cancelled.
- From stage 07 on, `toolkit work validate` warns when the Roadmap has no
  phase table, when Tasks has no checkbox lines, and when a template example
  row or task is left.
- Tick a task (`- [x]`, status Done) only with evidence: the test result
  line, the commit, or what the owner saw.
- A done or cancelled task is not reopened. Add a new task instead.
- A task whose "Done when" names the owner (for example "the owner confirms
  the wording") is not ticked by the agent. It becomes an Open Questions row
  with `owner` as who decides.
- A phase that a sub-item delivers lists the sub-item id in its Sub-items
  column. Finishing the sub-item does not finish or approve the parent.
- When the item is finished, every phase it completed says Done.

## 5. Tracking setup (stage 07)

Only what the item needs:

- **Branch and worktree** for code work: the worktree
  `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` on the branch
  `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, as the project's
  `.claude/rules/shared-repository-work.md` says. `toolkit work show <id>`
  prints the exact names. For WI-007:
  `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export`
  In Codex this Git write needs the owner's approval and escalated
  permissions (`git-rules.md`).
- **Salesforce projects:** the item's deployment folder
  `delivery/deployment/<work-item-id>-<short-name>/`, copied from
  `delivery/deployment/work-item-deployment-template/` and kept current by
  `sf-component-tracker`.
- **A test plan**, when the checks need more than the item's acceptance
  checks (several scenarios, a manual check, or a release): `work-check`
  writes it, in `tests/` on the item's branch.
- **Sub-items** for phases that own real scope: open `work-organize`.

## 6. Building (stage 08)

- Work on the item's own branch and worktree. Never on the default branch.
- One task at a time, in the order the Depends on lines allow.
- Commit with files staged by name and a plain message. No `Co-Authored-By`
  line naming an AI and no "Generated with" line (`git-rules.md`).
- With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per
  independent task, each with its own files. The main agent merges each
  builder's branch into the item's branch, checks the tests still pass, then
  ticks the task. Builders never change the work item.

  main agent makes its worktree and branch and names the folder in the
  brief; with approvals off, one builder at a time in the item's own worktree
  (`helpers.md`, section 2, "Codex builders").
- Tests go with each task. A check that could not run is reported as not
  run, never as passed.
- Salesforce: run `sf-component-tracker` after each metadata change. Anything
  that changes production data goes through `sf-data-change`; agents never
  write production data.
- The build shows a requirement is wrong or missing: stop that task, add an
  Open Questions row, and open `work-requirements`. Do not build around it.
- The build shows the design does not work: record it in the design's Notes
  and open `solution-design` for a design change.

## 7. Keeping the item current while building

After each task:

- tick it with evidence;
- update Overview Current position and Next action;
- add a history note only when something changed the plan.

The owner may edit the record while you build. Read the section again right
before you change it.

## 8. Checklist before stopping

Before the reply that ends a session with work unfinished:

- [ ] Overview Current position and Next action say where things stand.
- [ ] Notes > Resume here says exactly where to pick up.
- [ ] `waiting_on` is true: `owner` only while a question for him is open.
- [ ] One history note says what changed in this session.
- [ ] `toolkit work validate <id>` is clean.
- [ ] The current focus names the item and its real next step
      (`current-focus.md`).
- [ ] The reply ends with the one question for the owner, or the exact words
      that continue ("Say 'keep going' and I'll build P1.").

# Work check

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Checks a finished build against every requirement with an independent checker, fixes what fails, and asks the owner to approve the result; it never merges, deploys, or marks Done. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Find the item as `work-on` does: the id he named, this worktree's item, or a title that matches; two matches, ask one question naming both. Read the requirements, the Acceptance list, the Tasks, and the design's Acceptance checks; a sub-item with no design of its own is checked against its parent's (`references/testing.md`, section 1). Then set the testing stage.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work design <id>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 09-testing`
2. Run the project's tests and every acceptance check the item lists. Several scenarios or manual steps: write a test plan in `tests/` on the item's branch (`references/testing.md`, sections 2 and 3).
3. Brief the `acceptance-checker`, never the agent that built it, naming the branch and the exact commit (`references/testing.md`, section 4).
4. Failures: run the check and fix loop until clean, or until a failure needs an owner decision (`references/testing.md`, section 5).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 10-bug-fixing`
5. Record what was checked, the evidence, and the gaps.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Checked: <what>; evidence: <where>; gaps: <gaps or none>'`
6. Ask for the result approval with the checklist in `references/approvals.md`, section 4: stage 11, the item waiting on the owner, the result shown as "Showing the result" says below, and one question: "Do you approve this result?"
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 11-user-approval --waiting-on owner`
7. His yes: save his words first, record the approval, hand the item back to the agent, and open `work-finish`. A requirement change goes to `work-requirements`; a fix becomes a task and continues here.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Result approved; work-finish continues.'`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
8. Update the current focus when the item's next step changed (`references/current-focus.md`). End every reply with the approval question, or the exact words that continue.

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- The checker is never the agent or session that built the change. When no independent check could run, say so plainly before asking for approval.
- A check that did not run is reported as not run, never as passed.
- The test plan lives in `tests/` on the item's branch, committed there. Never in `.work-items/`, which Git ignores.
- "Looks good" to any question other than the approval question is not the approval. Ask the approval question.
- Add no Open Questions row for the result approval: stage 11 already lists it as the owner's decision.
- When the approve command fails, show the owner its error. Never work around it by editing the record.
- The result approval covers the result shown, never merge, deployment, or publishing; `work-finish` handles those.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Change the stage label and record the result in the issue (`references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`).

## Showing the result

- Lead with what the result does now, in the owner's terms: "The export button now creates a CSV file that opens in Excel."
- Then how he can see it himself: the link, the command to run, or a screenshot.
- Then the evidence: tests run and their result lines, the checker's verdicts.
- Then the gaps: anything partly met, not run, or known to be missing. Never hide a gap to get an approval.
- One question: "Do you approve this result?"

A "no": record his words, turn each named problem into a task or a requirement change, and continue.

## Agents

- `acceptance-checker` (`references/agent-acceptance-checker.md`): step 3 and every re-check.
- `builder` (`references/agent-builder.md`): fixes in step 4 when a team was recorded or the owner agreed; one builder per independent fix, one writer per path. In Codex the main agent first makes each builder's worktree (`references/helpers.md`, section 2, "Codex builders").
- Brief them as `references/helpers.md` says.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Give the full text of this skill's `references/agent-<name>.md`, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. # Testing a work item

How `work-check` decides what to check, writes a test plan when one is
needed, briefs the independent checker, runs the fix loop, and records the
result.

## Contents

1. What to check against
2. When a test plan is needed
3. Writing the test plan
4. Briefing the acceptance checker
5. The check and fix loop
6. Recording the result
7. Showing the result to the owner

## 1. What to check against

Read these before running anything:

- every `R-xx` block and its Acceptance check, and the item's Acceptance
  list: `toolkit work show <id>`;
- the design's "Build and verification plan" > Acceptance checks, and the
  selected option's "How to check it" column: `toolkit work design <id>`
  (it exits 1 when the item has no design);
- a sub-item whose show output says "Design: none of its own; WI-012's design
  is approved" is checked against the parent's design:
  `toolkit work design <parent-id>`;
- the Tasks section, to know what was built and on which branch.

## 2. When a test plan is needed

A test plan is needed when a check has several scenarios, a manual step, test
data, or a release across environments. The item's own acceptance checks are
enough when each one is a single automated test or a single observation.

## 3. Writing the test plan

- [ ] Work in the item's worktree, on its branch. Never on the default branch.
- [ ] Copy `tests/TEST-PLAN-TEMPLATE.md` to `tests/<id>-TEST-PLAN.md`, for
      example `tests/WI-012-TEST-PLAN.md`. Leave the template unchanged.
- [ ] Fill it as its guide comment says: Scope (the `R-xx` and items
      checked), Environment and data, one Checks row per scenario, then
      Results and follow-up. Delete the guide and the example row.
- [ ] Commit it on the item's branch with the results filled in, staged by
      name (`git-rules.md`).
- [ ] Never save it in `.work-items/`: Git ignores that folder, so the plan
      would never be committed.

One Checks row:

```markdown
| A manager clicks Export on the September report | A CSV file downloads and opens in Excel with all 12 columns | Manual, in the staging app | tests/evidence/wi-012-export.png |
```

## 4. Briefing the acceptance checker

The checker is never the agent or session that built the change. Brief the
`acceptance-checker` (Claude Code: `work:acceptance-checker`; Codex: the text
of `references/agent-acceptance-checker.md`) with, pasted in:

1. The item id.
2. The Agreed goal, every `R-xx` with its acceptance check, and the
   Acceptance list.
3. The design's Acceptance checks and the "How to check it" column.
4. The test plan, when there is one.
5. The branch and the exact commit to check.
6. The job: "Return one verdict per requirement (met, partly met, not met)
   with evidence, defects seen in the diff, and checks that could not run.
   Flag only gaps that affect correctness or the stated requirements."
7. Files it may write: nothing.

## 5. The check and fix loop

Repeat until clean, or until a failure needs the owner:

---
name: memory-save
description: 'Saves, corrects, or forgets one lasting fact in the project''s memory, or sends it to the record where it belongs. Use when the owner says "remember this", "from now on", "forget that", or "remind me" with no time given, corrects the agent, or a hook says a save is due.'
---

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Saves, corrects, or retires one memory record with `toolkit memory` commands, or sends the fact to its proper home. It never edits memory files by hand.

## Steps

Track these steps in the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

1. Decide the home with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory, which wins; otherwise `references/memory-criteria.md`). Not memory: send it to its home ("Where other things go" below) and stop.
2. Search for a record that already holds it, and read each hit with its version. The save's duplicate check compares wording, so only this search finds a record the new fact contradicts (for example "Mondays" against "Tuesdays").
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
   `toolkit memory get <key> --json`
3. Read the approval mode and apply "Approval policy" below. When it says ask, ask and wait.
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
4. Write the description and body in the record format (`references/record-format.md`), then save with the form for the case ("Save forms" below).
5. Exit code 2 saved nothing. Read the "Error:" line. Records listed: the duplicate check. "Changed since it was read": read it again and redo the change. Any other rule: fix the text as the message says. `references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 2, has each case.
6. "Forget that": retire the record, with his words as the reason. Delete only when his own words say delete ("Approval policy").
   `toolkit memory retire <key> --reason '<his words>'`
7. An owner to-do with no work item, or a change to what is happening now: update the current focus (`references/current-focus.md`). A project term: update the glossary (`references/glossary.md`).
8. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
9. Read the record back, check, and reply in one line ("Replies" below). End with the question still waiting for the owner, or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Approval policy

This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy.

- The owner's own words are the approval: "remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", or a correction. Save now, with `--approved-by <owner>`. That includes a fact about a named person he asks you to remember ("remember that Priya's last day is October 15").
- `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first, in exactly this form: "Save to memory: <one-line summary>?". Save after his yes (`references/proposals.md` when a proposal was saved for the question).
- `trusted` mode: a routine fact the agent is sure of is saved without asking and reported in one line, with no approver. The record says "Trusted grant".
- In either mode, always ask first for anything about a named person or personal details that he did not ask you to remember, for more than five records at once, and for a change to this policy.
- A delete needs his own words about that record ("delete it", "remove it for good"), or his yes to a numbered list that shows the delete. Do not ask again: the host asks him to confirm `toolkit memory delete`, and that prompt is the confirmation. "Forget that" is a retire, never a delete.
- A yes covers only the change and the meaning shown. Silence is never a yes.
- `--approved-by` is only for a change his words or his yes covered.
- An unanswered "Save to memory?" stays a proposal until he answers (`references/proposals.md`). Never drop it, and never save it with an approver.
- Only the owner switches the mode, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date, then run one of:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`

## Save forms

`<file>` is `-` in Claude Code, with the body on standard input after a quoted heredoc (`<<'EOF'`). In Codex give `--body '<text>'` in place of `--body-file <file>`. `references/record-format.md` shows both.

- A new record, from the owner's words or his yes:
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --approved-by <owner>`
- A new routine fact in `trusted` mode:
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>'`
- A question he has not answered yet:
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --proposal`
- An update of a record read in step 2, which his words or his yes covered:
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --expect <version> --approved-by <owner>`
- A routine update in `trusted` mode (the stored authorization is kept):
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --expect <version>`
- A new record that replaces an old one: add `--supersedes <old-key>` to a new-record form.
- A better name, or a type that matches the content:
  `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script. In Codex a joined command runs inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight, Notion, and the main checkout's `.memory/`.
- Put one-line values (`--description`, `--source`, `--reason`) in single quotes. An apostrophe inside them: Claude Code writes `'\''`; Codex writes ’ (U+2019) or rewords, and never uses `'\''`, which runs the command inside the sandbox. Double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`, drop that text, and the save still says "Saved".
- Never use a fixed file name such as `/tmp/memory.md`, and never write a file and run the command in one shell command.
- Body labels are bold paragraphs (`**Remember:**`), never `## Remember` headings.
- **Why** is the owner's reason in his words, or exactly "Not stated by the owner." Never a reason you inferred.
- In `onboarding` mode, a save with neither `--approved-by` nor `--proposal` is stored as "No approval recorded", and the save prints a "Note:" line about it. That is a mistake: fix it at once. Ask him, then save again with `--expect` and `--approved-by` after his yes, or with `--proposal` while he has not answered.
- A save of an existing key without `--expect` saves nothing. Take the version from the `--json` read; the first 12 characters are enough. Keep that read: its old text is the undo for an update.
- Add `--allow-similar` only after reading every record the duplicate check listed.
- A proposal the Stop hook saved holds only the one-line summary. His plain yes is `toolkit memory approve`, which takes out its "Do not rely on this" words; when he adds a reason or a detail, save the full body instead (`references/proposals.md`).
- Never store email addresses, secrets, or work-item status. The CLI catches common secret shapes, not all. For a secret, save where it is kept, never the secret.
- Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool.
- Built-in memory: the CLI rebuilds `MEMORY.md` and repairs links in other notes after a rename, supersede, retire, or delete, and names each note it changed. Read that report (`references/memory-builtin.md`).

## Where other things go

| The owner's words are about | Home | Open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project work, a task, a bug, "add it to the backlog" | A work item | `work-on` |
| A decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md` | `work-decide` |
| A requirement for a work item | The item's requirements | `work-requirements` |
| Behavior already delivered | `requirements/` | none |
| How a change is built | The item's design | `solution-design` |
| Verified current structure of the system | `system-guide/` | none |
| Outside documentation | `ai-external-knowledge/` | none |
| A standing rule for how agents work here | A rule-file change, proposed to him | none |
| His to-do with no work item and no time | Current focus, Untracked to-dos | step 7 |
| A to-do with a time ("at 9 tomorrow") | A scheduled reminder, outside memory | the host's scheduling tool |
| A project term | The glossary | step 7 |

A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy the record's body.

## Replies

Every memory reply ends with the next step: the question still waiting for the owner (for example "Save to memory: <one line>?"), or the exact words that continue. Never end on what was not done ("I haven't saved anything.").

- A new record: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo."
- An update: "Updated in memory: <title>. Say 'undo that' to put back the old wording." His "undo that" is a save of the old text from the `--json` read (`references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 3). Right after a supersede, the undo is a restore of the old record and a retire of the new one (same file, section 4).
- A proposal: "Saved as a proposal for your yes or no: <title>."
- A rejected proposal: "Not saved: <title>. I will not suggest it again.", then the next step.
- A retire: "Retired from memory: <title>. Say 'bring it back' to restore it." His "bring it back" is the whole restore in `references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 7, not `toolkit memory restore` alone.
- A delete: "Deleted from memory, as you said: '<his words>'. This cannot be undone." For a secret or an email address, add that older backups still hold it (`references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 8).
- A failed save: lead with "Not saved: <reason>." Keep the text and try again later in the session. With Hindsight or Notion, the command prints the fix (`references/memory-hindsight.md`, `references/memory-notion.md`).

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds one line when the owner's message holds one of six keep phrases: "remember that" (or "remember this"), "from now on", "don't ever", "note that", "going forward", or "keep in mind". It is a reminder: route the fact with step 1.
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase got no save, work-item change, or decision in the turn. Save it, or say in one line where it went instead.
- Ask in exactly the form "Save to memory: <one line>?" (bold is fine). Other wording, such as "Save it to memory?", makes the Stop hook stop the turn once and ask for that form.
- When a reply asks "Save to memory: <summary>?" and no proposal was saved in that turn, the Stop hook tries to save one, and the next turn's context says what happened:
  - It saved a proposal and names its key: his yes approves that key, his no rejects it (`references/proposals.md`, "Recording the owner's answer").
  - Memory already holds a proposal like it, and names it: his answer approves or rejects that proposal.
  - Memory already holds a record about the same subject, and names it: read it as in step 2. The same fact: keep it, or update it with `--expect`. A different fact and his yes: save it with `--allow-similar` and `--approved-by`. Never overwrite a record with a different fact.
  - The text looks like a secret, so nothing was saved: never save it; after his yes, save only where the secret is kept.
  - The save failed: save the proposal yourself in this turn, with `--proposal`.

| `references/memory-criteria.md` | Step 1, with Hindsight or Notion memory (built-in projects read `.memory/memory-criteria.md`) |
